title: Whose Homes Did His Roads Tear Down: Robert Moses's New York Legacy
dek: Moses used federal Title I money to demolish 26 blocks, pushing the poor from one slum to another, yet claimed 98% of relocatees ended up in better housing — and his legacy remains contested to this day.
why: This episode is medium-density, but the second half — on how power operates, media manipulation and the machinery of urban renewal — is worth hearing; the first half can be fast-forwarded.
who: Founders and investors interested in urban renewal, the exercise of infrastructure power, and the interplay of media and politics; engineers who want to understand how "strong execution" and "social cost" can coexist.
skip: The listener mail and pet photos starting at 36:54 can be skipped.

points.h: The more power you have, the less you need to explain
points.body: After LaGuardia retired in 1946, William O'Dwyer appointed Moses New York City Construction Coordinator, a post that gave him jurisdiction over every public construction project in the city and a direct line to Washington. By 1959, critics pointed out that he held multiple government positions at once and that his power was unchecked: consulting fees undisclosed, staff salaries undisclosed, trust meetings held behind closed doors, and land subject to arbitrary seizure. Reporter Bob Baum noted that private firms could do these things, but as part of a government entity, the public had a right to know. Moses was therefore often called the "construction czar" or "urban planning czar."

points.h: Roads first, and the price was whole neighborhoods
points.body: In 1948, Moses began building the Cross Bronx Expressway, a seven-mile road cutting through the already heavily developed Bronx. Dozens of apartment buildings were demolished, hundreds of families displaced, and many streets severed into dead ends. This fragmentation of the community was later cited as one reason for rising local crime rates. Those affected were mostly the least resourced, predominantly non-white communities. In a 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, Moses wrote that arterial improvements were "not merely a strip of pavement laid in a gasoline ditch, but a real improvement of the entire area," and he genuinely believed he was making the best choice for New York, but his methods were often ruthless.

points.h: 26 brochures, one act of visual persuasion
points.body: In 1949 Congress passed Title I of the U.S. Housing Act, providing $1 billion in loans and $100 million a year in grants for slum clearance. Moses realized New York could capture a large share of federal money, so in the 1950s he had his team produce 26 brochures, each targeting a neighborhood he believed needed redevelopment. The brochures contained problem descriptions, photographs and statistics, and were sent to the New York City Board of Estimate, the City Planning Commission, the federal Title I administrator and the Housing and Home Finance Agency. In 2014, researcher Temis Kronopoulos analyzed the photographs and found: vacant lots appeared 22 times, the most common image of urban decay; 20 photos showed back-alley garbage and clotheslines; and almost no people appeared in the photos. Kronopoulos wrote: "In this context, slum clearance was also a tool of social engineering."

points.h: The press praised him first, then the scandal broke
points.body: On June 29, 1959, New York Times reporter Wayne Phillips began publishing a four-part series exposing Moses's problems in Title I slum clearance projects: dealings with people he should not have been involved with, unmonitored funds, and information not shared. But as early as June 14, columns by George Sokolski began appearing in newspapers across the country, distributed by King Features Syndicate, with headlines like "Robert Moses Is a Selfless Man" and nearly identical content praising him for "constantly building and beautifying, his work never touched by graft or corruption." These articles ran two weeks before the New York Times's critical series. Looking back, Sokolski appears to have been asked to preemptively cover for the coming scandal.

points.h: The mayor's ban and a public temper tantrum
points.body: After the scandal broke, Mayor Wagner did two things: first, he investigated Louis Pokras's role in a Harlem slum clearance project, and because Pokras had organized crime ties, Wagner publicly said he would never allow him to sponsor any New York development project; second, he barred the city from working with Moses's favored architect, Melvin E. Kessler, whose earlier involvement in Upper West Side redevelopment saw developer Manhattan Town Incorporated take Title I money without building a single building or demolishing a single building, simply collecting rents while the buildings rotted. Moses responded publicly that the mayor's "devastating charges and misstatements" had scared off venture capital, and said "Title I is a dead duck." Other officials said Title I would continue and praised Moses. In the press coverage, Moses came across as throwing a public tantrum.

In December 1959, the Metropolitan Housing Council began distributing flyers in New York addressed to Mayor Robert Wagner. Across the top in bold letters: "For the sake of New York's development, Moses must go." The flyer listed the persistent problems of slum clearance projects: tenants sold along with the land; indecent relocation practices continuing; luxury housing built at the people's expense while those who needed housing most were pushed from one slum to another; and, as former rent administrator Charles Abrams pointed out, slum clearance had become "Negro and Puerto Rican removal." The flyer demanded: more low-rent housing, an end to subsidizing luxury housing, and building new housing before demolishing old. It compared the situation to cancer and repeated: "Moses must go."

points.h: The Fire Island showdown: Rockefeller accepted the resignation
points.body: In 1962, Moses clashed with New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller over a Fire Island road plan. Moses wanted to build a road running the length of the island, and after a 1962 storm destroyed most of the houses, he thought his chance had come. But environmental groups and islanders opposed it, and residents proposed making Fire Island a national seashore instead, winning federal support. Public pressure gave the governor an opening to halt the road project and to suggest Moses reduce his government posts to focus on the 1964 World's Fair. Moses submitted his resignation; he had threatened resignation before with other governors, but they had always refused, because many public projects would collapse without him. Rockefeller accepted, triggering a media storm. Moses claimed the governor had demanded he immediately resign as chairman of the State Parks Commission so that his brother Lawrence could take over; Rockefeller said a transition had been discussed for over a year.

points.h: The World's Fair: 50 million vs. a projected 70 million
points.body: The 1964 New York World's Fair drew about 50 million visitors, but Moses had projected 70 million. The New York Times reported that only 85% of the site was ready at opening, 15 of 139 pavilions were unfinished, and many completed pavilions had no exhibits. Some exhibitors arrived with nowhere to put their displays. A fair spokesman told the press that seeing all the other options would take more than a week, and the unfinished pavilions would be done before then. Some attractions were completed within weeks of opening; others were abandoned entirely. After the fair ended, Moses was no longer New York City Construction Coordinator. In September 1966, his wife Mary died after a long illness, and less than a month later Moses remarried Mary Grady, who worked as a secretary at the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority. In 1968, Rockefeller merged Triborough into another transportation agency and removed Moses, his last New York government post.

points.h: "The Power Broker": one book that set the terms for fifty years
points.body: In 1970, Moses published "Public Works: A Dangerous Trade," looking back on his career, and wrote: "History repeats itself. Sooner or later, as it has time and again, the opposition will quiet down and claim they were for the improvement all along." In 1974, journalist Robert Caro published "The Power Broker," detailing how Moses accumulated power and painting an overwhelmingly negative portrait; it became a bestseller. Moses issued a statement through his public relations team calling the book "full of errors, unsupported charges, malicious and baseless personal attacks, and wild swings at almost everyone in public life." He also said Caro had fabricated the notion of "helpless displaced people encountering a cruel public works dictator and being sadistically scattered into the worst slums," countering that 98% of those moved out of demolished neighborhoods got better housing. Caro's book won the Pulitzer Prize, and whether accurate or not, its portrayal of Moses has stuck ever since.

the point of writing about Robert Moses and what he does is to show that despite the materialism of current American life, there are still selfless men who serve the people, achieving great improvements in various fields without concern for private advance.

whether Robert Moses is right or wrong in what and the way he does things, whether he deserves an accolade of greatness or is just a puffed-up egoist, or whether, as some of his opponents contend, others could have done as well, are things that historians and students of tomorrow may examine in hard perspective.
